subject: Biotechnology
title: Gene Sequencing Technologies
description: A fast breakdown of Gene Sequencing Technologies for builders.

hook.text: Sanger sequencing read DNA one base at a time — today, next-gen sequencers read billions simultaneously.

buildup.text: Illumina sequencers fragment DNA into millions of pieces and read them all in parallel on a glass chip.

discovery.text: Nanopore sequencing threads DNA through a tiny hole — reading letters as they pass through, in real time.

twist.text: Oxford Nanopore's MinION fits in your hand — a pocket-sized sequencer used in jungles and space stations.

climax.text: Sequencing costs fell from $100 million to $200 per genome — faster than Moore's Law for two decades.

punchline.text: Reading DNA went from lab-only to pocket-sized in 20 years.

quiz.question: How does nanopore sequencing read DNA?
options: By shining lasers on fluorescent labels attached to each base
By threading DNA through a tiny pore and detecting each base as it passes
By breaking DNA into pieces and weighing each fragment

details.summary: Gene sequencing determines the exact order of nucleotide bases in a DNA molecule. Sanger sequencing reads individual fragments while next-generation sequencing processes millions simultaneously, enabling entire human genomes to be sequenced in hours for under a thousand dollars.
details.whyItMatters: Affordable rapid sequencing has transformed biology, enabling personalized medicine, pathogen tracking, ancestry analysis, and agricultural improvement. The cost of sequencing a human genome has dropped from 3 billion dollars to under a thousand.
takeaways: Sanger sequencing reads one DNA fragment at a time with high accuracy
Next-generation sequencing processes millions of fragments simultaneously
Human genome sequencing now costs under a thousand dollars and takes hours

faq.question: How has the cost of DNA sequencing changed over time?
faq.answer: The Human Genome Project spent about 3 billion dollars to sequence one genome by 2003. By 2014, it cost about a thousand dollars. Costs continue to drop faster than Moore's law, driven by advances in next-generation and nanopore sequencing technologies.

faq.question: What is the difference between Sanger and next-generation sequencing?
faq.answer: Sanger sequencing reads one fragment at a time with very high accuracy, suitable for small projects. NGS reads millions of fragments in parallel, trading individual read accuracy for massive throughput. Both generate complementary data depending on the application.
